title: competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition from rate data
stem:
An enzyme is assayed with and without a reversible inhibitor. Enzyme concentration, temperature and pH are the same in every tube. Initial rates (relative units per minute) are:
Substrate (mM) | No inhibitor | With inhibitor
2 | 33 | 14
4 | 50 | 25
10 | 71 | 45
40 | 91 | 77
200 | 98 | 94
Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The inhibitor is noncompetitive: it binds away from the active site and lowers the maximum rate at every substrate concentration.
choices.rationale: A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate, so the gap would remain large at 200 mM, but here the rates nearly converge (94 versus 98).

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inhibitor is competitive: it competes with the substrate for the active site, so a high substrate concentration nearly overcomes it.
choices.rationale: Correct: the rate gap shrinks from 19 units at 2 mM to 4 units at 200 mM and both curves approach the same maximum, which is the signature of competition for the active site.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The inhibitor permanently denatures a fraction of the enzyme molecules, so fewer enzyme molecules are available at every substrate concentration.
choices.rationale: Loss of active enzyme molecules would lower the maximum rate at saturating substrate too, and the rates would not converge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The inhibitor binds to the substrate and removes it from solution, so the rates fall by the same amount at every substrate concentration.
choices.rationale: The gap is not constant, since it falls from 19 to 4 units as substrate rises, which a fixed loss of substrate would not produce.

title: competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition from rate data (variant 1)
stem:
A second inhibitor is tested on the same enzyme under identical conditions. Initial rates (relative units per minute) are:
Substrate (mM) | No inhibitor | With inhibitor
2 | 33 | 17
4 | 50 | 25
10 | 71 | 36
40 | 91 | 45
200 | 98 | 49
A student proposes raising the substrate from 40 mM to 200 mM to restore the uninhibited rate. Which statement best evaluates the proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will succeed, because every inhibitor loses its effect once substrate is added in large excess.
choices.rationale: Only a competitive inhibitor is overcome by excess substrate, and this data shows a constant fractional reduction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will fail: the rate with inhibitor stays near half of the uninhibited rate at every substrate concentration, which fits an inhibitor that binds outside the active site and lowers the maximum rate.
choices.rationale: Correct: the inhibited rate is about 50 percent of the uninhibited rate at every concentration (17/33, 25/50, 36/71, 45/91, 49/98), so substrate cannot overcome it, as expected for a noncompetitive inhibitor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will fail only because the enzyme is denatured at high substrate concentration, which is why the rate stops rising.
choices.rationale: The uninhibited curve also levels off at high substrate because the enzyme is saturated, not denatured.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will succeed, because the rates at 2 mM and 4 mM show the inhibitor is weaker at higher substrate.
choices.rationale: The ratio of inhibited to uninhibited rate does not rise with substrate, so the inhibitor is not weaker at higher substrate.

title: competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition from rate data (variant 2)
stem: A drug has a shape and charge distribution similar to an enzyme's substrate and binds reversibly to the active site. In an assay containing 1 mM substrate and the drug, the rate is 30 percent of the uninhibited rate. A researcher raises the substrate concentration to 100 mM while keeping the drug concentration the same. Which prediction and explanation are best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The rate rises toward the uninhibited rate, because substrate and drug compete for the same active sites and more substrate occupies more of them.
choices.rationale: Correct: a reversible inhibitor that resembles the substrate and binds the active site is competitive, so its effect is reduced when substrate greatly outnumbers it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rate stays at about 30 percent, because the drug lowers the enzyme's maximum rate regardless of substrate.
choices.rationale: Lowering the maximum rate regardless of substrate describes noncompetitive inhibition, whereas this drug competes for the active site.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rate stays at about 30 percent, because the drug changes the shape of the active site by binding elsewhere on the enzyme.
choices.rationale: Binding elsewhere describes an allosteric or noncompetitive inhibitor, but the stem says the drug binds the active site.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rate rises toward the uninhibited rate, because extra substrate lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
choices.rationale: Substrate concentration does not change the activation energy, since only the enzyme and its structure do that.

title: competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition from rate data (variant 3)
stem:
Inhibitors X and Y each reduce the activity of the same enzyme. Initial rates (relative units per minute) at two substrate concentrations are:
Condition | 10 mM substrate | 100 mM substrate
No inhibitor | 60 | 94
Inhibitor X | 45 | 89
Inhibitor Y | 30 | 47
Which interpretation is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are competitive, because both lower the rate at 10 mM substrate.
choices.rationale: Every inhibitor lowers the rate at some concentration, so that observation cannot distinguish the types; the 100 mM data can.

choices.label: B
choices.text: X is likely noncompetitive because it lowers the rate at 10 mM, while Y is likely competitive because it lowers the rate more.
choices.rationale: The larger drop at low substrate does not identify a type, and the rate with Y does not recover, which is the noncompetitive pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.text: X is likely competitive because 100 mM substrate nearly restores the rate, while Y is likely noncompetitive because the rate stays about half of normal.
choices.rationale: Correct: with X the rate recovers from 75 percent to 95 percent of normal as substrate rises, while with Y it stays near 50 percent, so X behaves competitively and Y noncompetitively.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both are noncompetitive, because neither reaches the uninhibited rate at 100 mM.
choices.rationale: X comes within about 5 percent of the uninhibited rate at 100 mM, which is consistent with competition and not with a fixed loss of capacity.

title: choose the control isolating enzyme activity
stem: A student grinds potato tissue and filters the liquid. When she adds 1 mL of the extract to hydrogen peroxide, bubbles form quickly. She claims that an enzyme in the extract causes the bubbling. Which additional treatment would best test whether the bubbling depends on the enzyme's native, folded structure rather than on some other component of the extract?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add 1 mL of the same extract that was first heated in boiling water and then cooled, to the same hydrogen peroxide solution.
choices.rationale: Correct: boiled extract contains the same chemical components but has denatured proteins, so if bubbling stops the difference must be due to the folded protein.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add 1 mL of extract to water in place of hydrogen peroxide.
choices.rationale: This shows whether the extract alone releases gas, but it does not separate enzyme activity from other extract components when peroxide is present.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add 2 mL of the untreated extract to the same hydrogen peroxide solution.
choices.rationale: Doubling the amount is a dose comparison that changes a variable and cannot show that the activity depends on protein structure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add 1 mL of the untreated extract to a hydrogen peroxide solution at a lower concentration.
choices.rationale: Changing the peroxide concentration tests a substrate effect and does not distinguish an enzyme from other components of the extract.

title: choose the control isolating enzyme activity (variant 1)
stem: A student adds pancreatic extract to milk containing an indicator that turns from pink to colorless as fatty acids form. The color fades within minutes, and she claims lipase in the extract is responsible. Which control best shows that the change depends on an active, properly folded enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the same amount of extract with the milk adjusted to a different pH.
choices.rationale: Changing the pH introduces a second variable and tests a pH effect, not the dependence on enzyme structure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use ice-cold milk with the same amount of untreated extract.
choices.rationale: Lowering the temperature slows an enzyme without destroying it, so a slow color change would not show that the protein structure is responsible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use the same amount of extract that was heated to denature its proteins and then cooled to the same temperature.
choices.rationale: Correct: the heated extract keeps every other component but loses folded protein, so persistence of the pink color would show the change depends on active enzyme.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use the same amount of extract with a larger volume of milk.
choices.rationale: Changing the milk volume changes the substrate amount and says nothing about whether the active enzyme is required.

title: choose the control isolating enzyme activity (variant 2)
stem: An inhibitor is dissolved in the solvent DMSO. When 20 microliters of the inhibitor solution is added to an assay, the rate of the reaction falls from 50 to 20 units per minute. Which control best shows that the decrease is caused by the inhibitor and not by the solvent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An assay with the inhibitor solution but with no substrate.
choices.rationale: Without substrate there is no reaction to measure, so this assay cannot show what the solvent does to the rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An assay with twice the amount of inhibitor solution.
choices.rationale: Doubling the dose tests whether the effect increases with dose, but it still contains the solvent, so it cannot separate solvent from inhibitor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An assay with 20 microliters of DMSO that contains no inhibitor.
choices.rationale: Correct: the solvent-only assay matches everything except the inhibitor, so if the rate stays near 50 the inhibitor and not the solvent caused the drop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An assay with no enzyme but with the inhibitor solution.
choices.rationale: Without the enzyme the reaction rate says nothing about how the solvent affects the enzyme.

title: choose the control isolating enzyme activity (variant 3)
stem: A student uses the iodine test, which turns blue-black with starch, to detect amylase activity in saliva. Before testing saliva she wants to confirm that her assay can detect starch breakdown at all. Which tube is the best positive control?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Starch solution with boiled saliva, then iodine.
choices.rationale: Boiled saliva is a negative control because its enzyme is denatured and no starch breakdown is expected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Starch solution with water instead of saliva, then iodine.
choices.rationale: Starch with water is a negative control that shows what no breakdown looks like.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water with saliva, with no starch, then iodine.
choices.rationale: There is no starch in this tube, so no breakdown is possible and the tube does not test the assay's ability to detect it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Starch solution with a commercial amylase solution known to be active, then iodine.
choices.rationale: Correct: a positive control uses a treatment known to produce the effect; active amylase with starch should lose the blue-black color if the assay works.

title: predict allosteric feedback inhibition in a pathway
stem: In a bacterial biosynthetic pathway, enzyme E1 converts substrate A to B, E2 converts B to C, and E3 converts C to the end product D. D binds reversibly to a site on E1 that is separate from the active site. A researcher adds excess D to a cell extract that contains all three enzymes and plenty of A. Which prediction and explanation are best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The rate of conversion of A to B increases, because D is a product of the pathway and more D pulls the pathway forward.
choices.rationale: Products of the pathway inhibit the early enzyme rather than stimulating it, which is how the cell avoids overproduction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rate of conversion of A to B stays the same, because D can act only on E3, the enzyme that makes it.
choices.rationale: The stem says D binds E1, so D acts on the first step and not only on E3.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rate of conversion of A to B falls, because D binds a site other than the active site and changes the shape of E1, which reduces its activity.
choices.rationale: Correct: feedback inhibition by an end product that binds an allosteric site shuts down the first step, which prevents the cell from wasting resources on excess D.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rate of conversion of A to B falls, because D competes with A for the active site, so raising A would fully restore the rate.
choices.rationale: D binds a site separate from the active site, so it does not compete with A, and added A would not fully restore the rate.

title: predict allosteric feedback inhibition in a pathway (variant 1)
stem: In the same pathway (E1 makes B from A, E2 makes C from B, E3 makes D from C, and D inhibits E1 allosterically), a cell is growing with a moderate level of D that partly inhibits E1. A drug then completely and irreversibly blocks E2. Which change is most likely over the next few minutes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A accumulates and B falls, because the drug blocks E1.
choices.rationale: The drug acts on E2, and E1 becomes more active as D falls, so A would be consumed and not accumulate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: C accumulates, because C is made by E2 even when E2 is blocked.
choices.rationale: C is produced only by E2, so with E2 blocked its supply stops and it does not accumulate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All intermediates fall, because blocking one enzyme shuts down every reaction in the pathway at once.
choices.rationale: The product of the unblocked first enzyme, B, builds up, so not every intermediate falls.

choices.label: D
choices.text: D falls, so inhibition of E1 is relieved and B accumulates because E2 can no longer remove it.
choices.rationale: Correct: blocking E2 stops the production of C and D, so the inhibitor D falls and E1 speeds up, while B is made faster and not removed.

title: predict allosteric feedback inhibition in a pathway (variant 2)
stem: A mutant bacterium has an E1 whose active site is unchanged but which can no longer bind the end product D at its regulatory site. Compared with the normal strain growing under the same conditions, which prediction is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mutant makes less D, because the mutation weakened the active site of E1.
choices.rationale: The stem states the active site is unchanged, and the lost feature is the regulatory binding site.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mutant makes the same amount of D, because regulatory sites never affect enzyme activity.
choices.rationale: Binding at a regulatory site normally lowers the enzyme's activity, so losing it changes the amount of D made.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mutant stops making D, because without regulation the pathway cannot run.
choices.rationale: The pathway still runs because the active site works, and the loss of feedback lets it run unchecked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mutant accumulates much more D, because E1 stays active even when D is abundant.
choices.rationale: Correct: with the regulatory site unable to bind D, feedback is lost, so E1 continues to work at a high rate and D builds up.

title: predict allosteric feedback inhibition in a pathway (variant 3)
stem: An enzyme that catalyzes the first step of a pathway has an activity of 100 units in the absence of the end product P and 20 units when P is present. After the sample is dialyzed to remove P, the activity returns to 95 units. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P permanently denatures the enzyme, which is why activity falls.
choices.rationale: Permanent denaturation would prevent the activity from returning when P is removed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: P is used up as a substrate by the enzyme, which is why activity falls.
choices.rationale: If P were consumed as a substrate, activity would rise and not fall when P is present.

choices.label: C
choices.text: P covalently modifies the enzyme and the dialysis removes the modification.
choices.rationale: Dialysis removes small free molecules and cannot reverse covalent changes, so the recovery points to reversible binding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: P binds the enzyme reversibly and alters its activity without permanently damaging the enzyme.
choices.rationale: Correct: activity recovered to 95 percent once P was removed, which means that P binds reversibly and does not destroy the enzyme.

title: interpret rate vs temperature/pH data for enzymes with different optima
stem:
A researcher measures the initial rate of a similar reaction catalyzed by an enzyme from a human cell and an enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium. Substrate concentration and pH are identical in all tests.
Temperature (°C) | Human enzyme rate | Hot-spring enzyme rate
20 | 6 | 1
37 | 20 | 3
60 | 2 | 12
80 | 0 | 20
95 | 0 | 4
Which statement is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each rate rises with temperature up to the enzyme's optimum and then falls as heat disrupts the active site, and the hot-spring enzyme's optimum is much higher than the human enzyme's.
choices.rationale: Correct: the human enzyme peaks near 37°C and the hot-spring enzyme near 80°C; below the optimum low rates reflect low kinetic energy, above it they reflect loss of active-site shape.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hot-spring enzyme is denatured at 20°C and 37°C, which is why its rates there are low.
choices.rationale: Cool temperatures slow molecular motion and collisions but do not denature a protein, so the low rate at 20°C does not indicate denaturation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The human enzyme's rate falls above 37°C because the substrate is used up at higher temperatures.
choices.rationale: The stem holds the substrate concentration the same, and the decline at high temperature comes from loss of the active-site shape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hot-spring enzyme has a higher rate at every temperature tested because it comes from an extremophile.
choices.rationale: The human enzyme has higher rates at 20°C and 37°C (6 and 20 versus 1 and 3), so the claim of a higher rate at every temperature is false.

title: interpret rate vs temperature/pH data for enzymes with different optima (variant 1)
stem:
The activities of pepsin (found in the stomach) and trypsin (found in the small intestine) are measured at several pH values with temperature and substrate constant.
pH | Pepsin rate | Trypsin rate
2 | 10 | 0
5 | 2 | 3
8 | 0 | 10
11 | 0 | 1
Which explanation best accounts for these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pepsin cannot function at pH 8 because there are no hydrogen ions available to act as its substrate.
choices.rationale: Hydrogen ions are not the substrate of these enzymes, and pepsin loses activity at high pH because of altered structure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two enzymes have the same optimum, and the differences between them are measurement error.
choices.rationale: The peaks are far apart (pH 2 versus pH 8) and the pattern is clear, so the difference reflects different structures and not error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trypsin is inactive at pH 2 because the acid hydrolyzes its peptide bonds and permanently cuts the polypeptide.
choices.rationale: A brief exposure to pH 2 changes side-chain charge and shape, but it does not break peptide bonds, so the explanation by hydrolysis is incorrect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: pH changes the ionization of amino acid side chains, which alters the interactions that maintain the active site, so each enzyme works best near the pH of its own environment.
choices.rationale: Correct: pepsin peaks at pH 2 and trypsin at pH 8, matching the stomach and intestine; pH affects R-group charge and therefore the shape and binding of the active site.

title: interpret rate vs temperature/pH data for enzymes with different optima (variant 2)
stem:
The initial rate of an enzyme at pH 7 and several temperatures is measured:
Temperature (°C) | Rate (relative units)
10 | 4
20 | 8
30 | 15
40 | 3
Which prediction for 25°C and 50°C is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At 25°C the rate is between 3 and 8, and at 50°C it is above 15.
choices.rationale: The rate at 25°C must fall between the values at 20°C and 30°C, and it cannot be below 8, while the high rate at 50°C ignores the collapse seen at 40°C.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At 25°C the rate is above 15, and at 50°C it is between 8 and 15.
choices.rationale: The rate at 25°C cannot exceed the 30°C value of 15 when the trend is rising, and 50°C would not recover to a mid-level rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At 25°C the rate is between 8 and 15, and at 50°C it is below 3 because even more of the enzyme is denatured.
choices.rationale: Correct: the rate rises from 20°C to 30°C, so 25°C lies between 8 and 15; the rate already collapses at 40°C from heat damage, so more damage at 50°C gives an even lower rate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At 25°C the rate is between 8 and 15, and at 50°C it stays near 15 because kinetic energy keeps rising.
choices.rationale: Increasing kinetic energy does not help once the active site is distorted, as the fall at 40°C shows.

title: interpret rate vs temperature/pH data for enzymes with different optima (variant 3)
stem:
An enzyme is assayed at two temperatures and two substrate concentrations. Enzyme amount and pH are identical.
Temperature | 1 mM substrate | 50 mM substrate
25°C | 10 | 40
55°C | 1 | 3
A student proposes to rescue the activity at 55°C by adding more substrate. Which evaluation is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will not help much: at 55°C the maximum rate is lowered because much of the enzyme has lost its active-site shape, and more substrate cannot restore the lost enzyme.
choices.rationale: Correct: even at 50 mM substrate the rate at 55°C is only 3 compared with 40 at 25°C, so the limit is the amount of functional enzyme and not the substrate supply.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will fully restore activity, because substrate concentration alone limits every enzyme.
choices.rationale: Raising substrate helps only if substrate is limiting, and the rate at 55°C stays low even at 50 mM, which shows the enzyme is the limit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will help because higher substrate concentrations make the active site refold.
choices.rationale: Substrate does not cause a denatured protein to refold, and the data show no recovery.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will not help, because substrate cannot bind a heated enzyme at all.
choices.rationale: The rate rises from 1 to 3 with more substrate, so some functional enzyme still binds substrate, and the issue is that most of it is lost.

title: identify and fix a design flaw in an enzyme environment experiment
stem: A student measures catalase activity in potato at 5, 20, 35 and 60°C by placing a potato disc in hydrogen peroxide and counting oxygen bubbles for one minute. Because she ran short, she used 3 percent hydrogen peroxide at 5°C and 20°C but 5 percent at 35°C and 60°C. All other conditions were identical. Which change would most improve the validity of her conclusion about temperature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a different potato at each temperature so that differences between potatoes average out.
choices.rationale: Using a different potato at each temperature adds a second variable and cannot be averaged out with one trial per temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use the same hydrogen peroxide concentration in every tube so that temperature is the only variable that differs.
choices.rationale: Correct: the substrate concentration differs between tubes, so a rate difference between 20°C and 35°C could come from the concentration change and not from temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the peroxide concentration further as temperature rises to compensate for the faster collisions.
choices.rationale: Adjusting concentration with temperature creates an even larger confounded difference between tubes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a different buffer in each tube so that pH rises with the temperature.
choices.rationale: Changing the pH across the tubes adds another variable and makes the effect of temperature harder to isolate.

title: identify and fix a design flaw in an enzyme environment experiment (variant 1)
stem:
A student measures the product formed after 30 minutes by an enzyme at five temperatures, starting with 100 micromoles of substrate in every tube.
Temperature | Product at 30 min (micromoles)
5°C | 20
20°C | 100
35°C | 100
50°C | 100
70°C | 40
She concludes that the enzyme works equally well from 20 to 50°C. Which change would best improve the experiment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run all tubes for 60 minutes so the lower temperatures can catch up.
choices.rationale: A longer run makes the end-point problem worse, because even more tubes would be at the same completed endpoint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Remove the 70°C tube because it does not fit the trend.
choices.rationale: Removing data that does not fit is poor practice, and the 70°C tube carries real information about heat damage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measure product at several early time points and compare initial rates, before the substrate is used up.
choices.rationale: Correct: the three tubes all converted every micromole of substrate, so the end point hides rate differences; initial rates would reveal which temperature is fastest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Double the starting substrate in every tube so that the reaction lasts longer in each tube.
choices.rationale: The problem is that a single late measurement hides the rates, and doubling the substrate still leaves one end-point reading that does not reveal which temperature is fastest.

title: identify and fix a design flaw in an enzyme environment experiment (variant 2)
stem: A student tests the effect of pH on an enzyme. Tubes at pH 4, 7 and 10 are prepared. The pH 4 tube is kept on ice until the assay, the pH 7 tube is at room temperature, and the pH 10 tube is warmed to 37°C, because that is what was convenient. Initial rates are 3, 15 and 6. Which change would best allow a valid conclusion about pH?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a larger number of different pH values and keep the original temperatures.
choices.rationale: More pH values do not fix the confounding because each would still carry a different temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bring all tubes to the same temperature before adding the enzyme so that pH is the only variable that differs.
choices.rationale: Correct: temperature differs between tubes, so rate differences cannot be assigned to pH until all tubes share one temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use a fresh enzyme sample at each pH and keep the original temperatures.
choices.rationale: Fresh enzyme at each pH does not change that the tubes differ in temperature, and the confounding remains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run only the pH 7 tube at 37°C because that is closest to body temperature.
choices.rationale: Testing only one tube at 37°C does not give a comparison across pH and does not remove the differing temperatures from the other tubes.

title: identify and fix a design flaw in an enzyme environment experiment (variant 3)
stem: A student measures the rate of an enzyme at 30°C and at 35°C using one tube at each temperature. The rates are 12.0 and 12.8 units. She concludes that the enzyme is more active at 35°C. Which change would best strengthen the conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run several replicate tubes at each temperature and compare the means and the spread of the replicates.
choices.rationale: Correct: a difference of 0.8 units from single tubes could be within normal variation, and replicates allow the difference to be judged against the spread.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the temperature difference to 3°C by repeating the 35°C tube at 38°C.
choices.rationale: Changing the 35°C condition to 38°C does not address whether the original difference was real, and it changes the variable under test.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use only the 35°C tube, since it had the higher rate.
choices.rationale: Dropping the 30°C tube removes the comparison that the claim depends on.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to a higher substrate concentration in the 35°C tube only.
choices.rationale: Raising substrate only in one tube adds a second variable and makes the comparison invalid.

title: net free-energy change of coupled reactions; catalysis vs coupling
stem: A cell converts compound X to compound Y in a reaction with a free-energy change of +20 kJ/mol. The hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate has a free-energy change of −30 kJ/mol. An enzyme couples the two by transferring the terminal phosphate of ATP to X. Which prediction is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of −50 kJ/mol, because the two magnitudes add.
choices.rationale: The values must be added with their signs, and adding magnitudes treats an energy cost as a gain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of −10 kJ/mol, so it can proceed spontaneously.
choices.rationale: Correct: the free-energy changes of coupled reactions add algebraically, +20 + (−30) = −10 kJ/mol, which is negative, so the overall process is spontaneous.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The coupled reaction keeps a free-energy change of +20 kJ/mol, so it still does not proceed.
choices.rationale: Coupling changes the overall free-energy change because the ATP hydrolysis is part of the coupled reaction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of +50 kJ/mol, because the ATP hydrolysis adds a cost.
choices.rationale: ATP hydrolysis is exergonic and contributes a negative value, so it lowers the total and does not raise it.

title: net free-energy change of coupled reactions; catalysis vs coupling (variant 1)
stem: A reaction has a free-energy change of +35 kJ/mol and is coupled by an enzyme to the hydrolysis of one ATP (−30 kJ/mol) under the same conditions. Which prediction is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coupled reaction proceeds, because any exergonic reaction drives any endergonic reaction.
choices.rationale: The coupled process proceeds only if the sum of the free-energy changes is negative, which is not the case here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The coupled reaction has an overall change of −30 kJ/mol, because the more negative step determines the result.
choices.rationale: The sum is +35 − 30, and the larger value does not simply dominate by being more negative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The coupled reaction is spontaneous because the enzyme lowers the activation energy.
choices.rationale: An enzyme lowers activation energy but does not change the free-energy change, so it cannot make a positive net value spontaneous.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coupled reaction has an overall change of +5 kJ/mol and would not proceed, but coupling to two ATP (−60 kJ/mol) would give −25 kJ/mol.
choices.rationale: Correct: +35 − 30 = +5 kJ/mol, which is positive; adding a second ATP hydrolysis gives +35 − 60 = −25 kJ/mol, which is negative.

title: net free-energy change of coupled reactions; catalysis vs coupling (variant 2)
stem: In a cell, the formation of ATP from ADP and phosphate has a free-energy change of +30 kJ/mol. An enzyme couples this to the breakdown of phosphoenolpyruvate, which releases −62 kJ/mol. Which statement is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of +92 kJ/mol, so ATP cannot form.
choices.rationale: The +92 value comes from subtracting the sign of an exergonic reaction, whereas it contributes a negative term.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of −32 kJ/mol, so ATP formation can proceed.
choices.rationale: Correct: −62 + 30 = −32 kJ/mol, which is negative, so ATP synthesis driven by this reaction can proceed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of −62 kJ/mol, because the breakdown of phosphoenolpyruvate is unaffected by the coupling.
choices.rationale: The two free-energy changes add to give a single value, and the reaction with positive value contributes to it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of −30 kJ/mol, because ATP formation always releases energy.
choices.rationale: ATP formation from ADP and phosphate requires an energy input and has a positive free-energy change.

title: net free-energy change of coupled reactions; catalysis vs coupling (variant 3)
stem: An enzyme is added to a solution of X, which converts to Y in a reaction with a free-energy change of +20 kJ/mol. No ATP is present. Which prediction about the reaction after a long time is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The enzyme makes the reaction spontaneous because it lowers the activation energy, so most X becomes Y.
choices.rationale: Lowering activation energy changes speed only, and the free-energy change that sets the equilibrium is unchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The enzyme speeds the approach to equilibrium and shifts the equilibrium toward Y, so at equilibrium most of the material is Y.
choices.rationale: An enzyme does not shift the equilibrium, because it speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally and leaves the free-energy difference between X and Y unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The enzyme supplies energy from its own bonds, so the reaction proceeds until all X is gone.
choices.rationale: Enzymes are not consumed and do not donate energy from their own bonds to drive reactions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The enzyme speeds the approach to equilibrium, but at equilibrium most of the material is still X because the enzyme does not change the free-energy change.
choices.rationale: Correct: a catalyst changes the rate and not the free-energy change or the equilibrium position, so the reaction with ΔG = +20 kJ/mol still favors X.

title: ATP cycling: use and regeneration, with perturbations
stem: In skeletal muscle, the concentration of ATP is about 5.0 mM at rest and about 4.8 mM during intense contraction, even though the rate of ATP hydrolysis is about 20 times higher during contraction. Which explanation best accounts for the nearly constant ATP concentration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ADP and phosphate produced by hydrolysis are rapidly converted back to ATP using energy from fuel oxidation, so synthesis keeps pace with use.
choices.rationale: Correct: a constant concentration at a higher rate of hydrolysis means regeneration also speeds up; the cell resynthesizes ATP from ADP and phosphate using energy from catabolism.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Muscle cells store a very large pool of ATP, and hydrolysis during contraction takes ATP from it without any replacement.
choices.rationale: The muscle holds only a small ATP pool, which would be used up within seconds of intense work, so a replacement is essential.

choices.label: C
choices.text: ATP hydrolysis releases energy that creates new ATP molecules directly, so the pool is replaced by hydrolysis itself.
choices.rationale: Hydrolysis releases energy but does not make ATP, and ATP synthesis requires energy from the breakdown of fuels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Contraction uses energy directly from glucose and not from ATP, so ATP hydrolysis hardly affects the pool.
choices.rationale: The stem states hydrolysis is 20 times higher in contraction, and energy from glucose is first transferred to ATP.

title: ATP cycling: use and regeneration, with perturbations (variant 1)
stem: Cultured cells are grown on a medium that forces them to make ATP only by ATP synthase in mitochondria. A researcher adds oligomycin, which blocks ATP synthase, and then monitors the cells. Compared with untreated cells, which change is most likely over the next few minutes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ratio of ATP to ADP rises, because ATP hydrolysis stops when ATP synthase is blocked.
choices.rationale: The enzymes that use ATP are not blocked, so hydrolysis continues and the ATP concentration falls.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ratio of ATP to ADP stays the same, because cells hold ATP in lipid droplets for later use.
choices.rationale: Cells do not keep a large ATP reserve in lipid droplets, and the small ATP pool turns over quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ratio of ATP to ADP falls, but active transport speeds up because more ADP is available to power it.
choices.rationale: ADP does not power transport, which needs energy released by hydrolysis of ATP, so transport slows as ATP falls.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ratio of ATP to ADP falls because ATP use continues, and energy-requiring processes such as active transport slow down.
choices.rationale: Correct: with no way to regenerate ATP, continued hydrolysis lowers the ATP to ADP ratio, and processes that use ATP slow as the supply falls.

title: ATP cycling: use and regeneration, with perturbations (variant 2)
stem: A resting adult has about 50 g of ATP in the body at any moment but hydrolyzes about 50 kg of ATP per day. Which statement best reconciles these numbers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The body makes 50 kg of new ATP each day from nothing, using energy absorbed from the environment.
choices.rationale: ATP is built from ADP and phosphate with energy from fuel oxidation, and not from nothing or the environment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only 50 g of ATP is hydrolyzed each day, and the 50 kg estimate counts the same energy several times.
choices.rationale: The question gives the rate of hydrolysis as 50 kg per day, and recycling lets the same molecules be hydrolyzed repeatedly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each ATP molecule is recycled about 1,000 times a day, because ADP and phosphate are converted back to ATP using energy from food molecules.
choices.rationale: Correct: 50 kg divided by 50 g is 1,000, so each molecule is used and regenerated about 1,000 times per day; regeneration uses energy released from catabolism.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The body stores 50 kg of ATP in the liver, and only 50 g is in use at one time.
choices.rationale: ATP is not stored in large amounts in any organ because it is unstable, so the explanation is recycling, not storage.

title: ATP cycling: use and regeneration, with perturbations (variant 3)
stem: Vesicles containing a calcium pump are placed in a solution with calcium. With ATP, calcium accumulates inside the vesicles. With AMP-PNP, an analog that binds the pump like ATP but cannot be hydrolyzed, no calcium accumulates. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of a nucleotide to the pump supplies the energy for transport.
choices.rationale: The analog binds the pump yet produces no transport, so binding by itself is not the energy source.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transport needs the energy released when the terminal phosphate bond of ATP is hydrolyzed, and not only the binding of a nucleotide.
choices.rationale: Correct: the analog binds but is not hydrolyzed and gives no transport, so the energy for transport comes from the hydrolysis step.

choices.label: C
choices.text: AMP-PNP denatures the pump before transport can occur.
choices.rationale: The stem says the analog binds the pump like ATP, and nothing suggests denaturation, so the lack of hydrolysis is the key difference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: ATP acts as an enzyme that lowers the activation energy for calcium movement.
choices.rationale: ATP is a substrate and energy carrier, and the pump is the enzyme, so ATP does not act as an enzyme here.

title: interpret DCPIP/leaf-disc/stroma experiments separating light-dependent steps
stem:
Isolated chloroplast suspensions are mixed with DCPIP, a blue dye that becomes colorless when it accepts electrons. Absorbance (higher means bluer, more unreduced DCPIP) is measured at the start (0.80 in every tube) and after 10 minutes.
Tube | Treatment | Absorbance at 10 min
1 | Intact chloroplasts, light | 0.25
2 | Intact chloroplasts, dark | 0.78
3 | Boiled chloroplasts, light | 0.79
4 | Intact chloroplasts, light, plus DCMU (blocks electron flow from photosystem II) | 0.77
Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DCPIP is reduced by electrons from light-driven electron transport in intact thylakoids, which needs light, intact membranes and working photosystem II.
choices.rationale: Correct: only tube 1 loses blue color; without light, with denatured chloroplasts, or with electron flow blocked, absorbance stays near 0.80.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fall in absorbance in tube 1 shows that the Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ in the light.
choices.rationale: No CO₂ was supplied or measured, and DCPIP reduction reports electron flow in the light reactions and not carbon fixation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: DCPIP is reduced slightly in tubes 2 to 4 and more in tube 1, so light is helpful but not required.
choices.rationale: The changes in tubes 2 to 4 (0.02, 0.01, 0.03) are very small and consistent with no reduction, so light is required.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tube 3 shows that light alone is enough to reduce DCPIP, even in the absence of functional chloroplasts.
choices.rationale: Tube 3 contains light but its absorbance barely changes, which shows light alone does not reduce DCPIP.

title: interpret DCPIP/leaf-disc/stroma experiments separating light-dependent steps (variant 1)
stem: The same DCPIP assay is run with intact chloroplasts in the dark and under equal intensities of red, green or blue light. Absorbance (initial 0.80) after 10 minutes is: dark 0.78, red 0.30, blue 0.28, green 0.70. Which interpretation is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Green light is absorbed most strongly by chlorophyll, because it produces the largest drop in absorbance.
choices.rationale: Green gives the smallest drop in absorbance of the three colors, so it is the least effective, and the largest drop is with red and blue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Green light drives no electron flow at all, because chlorophyll cannot absorb any green light.
choices.rationale: The absorbance in green falls by 0.10 versus 0.02 in the dark, which shows some electron flow, so absorption is weak and not absent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Red and blue light drive much more electron transport than green, because chlorophylls absorb red and blue strongly and green weakly; the small drop in green shows some absorption.
choices.rationale: Correct: the drop is 0.50 (red), 0.52 (blue) and 0.10 (green) compared with 0.02 in the dark, so green is used but poorly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The three colors drive equal electron flow, and the differences are due to the dye.
choices.rationale: The three drops differ by a factor of about five, which is too large to attribute to the dye.

title: interpret DCPIP/leaf-disc/stroma experiments separating light-dependent steps (variant 2)
stem:
Leaf discs from which air has been removed sink in solution. A student places discs in three conditions and records the time for the first disc to float, which happens when oxygen accumulates in the disc.
Condition | Result
Bright light, bicarbonate solution | floats at 8 minutes
Bright light, plain water | no discs float by 30 minutes
Darkness, bicarbonate solution | no discs float by 30 minutes
Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bicarbonate supplies the energy that drives the light reactions.
choices.rationale: Bicarbonate supplies carbon dioxide for the Calvin cycle, and light, not bicarbonate, supplies the energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Floating depends on oxygen accumulating from photosynthesis, which in these discs needs both light and bicarbonate as a CO₂ source.
choices.rationale: Correct: floating happens only with both light and bicarbonate, so the oxygen buildup depends on photosynthesis with a CO₂ supply.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discs in darkness make oxygen by respiration, but too slowly to make them float.
choices.rationale: Respiration consumes oxygen and does not produce it, so the dark disc cannot gain oxygen by respiration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxygen release depends only on light, because oxygen comes from splitting water, so bicarbonate only changes how buoyant the discs are.
choices.rationale: The discs in plain water had the same light but did not float, so oxygen accumulation does depend on a CO₂ supply, because the Calvin cycle regenerates the NADP⁺ and ADP the light reactions need.

title: interpret DCPIP/leaf-disc/stroma experiments separating light-dependent steps (variant 3)
stem:
Isolated chloroplast stroma (with the Calvin cycle enzymes but no thylakoids) is incubated in the dark with ¹⁴CO₂. The amount of radioactive carbon incorporated into sugar after 10 minutes is:
Additions | ¹⁴C in sugar
None | 1
ATP only | 2
NADPH only | 2
ATP and NADPH | 60
Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The carbon-fixing reactions do not need light directly, but they need both ATP and NADPH, which the light reactions normally supply.
choices.rationale: Correct: only the combination of ATP and NADPH restores sugar synthesis in the dark, so both are required, and light acts indirectly through the light reactions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The carbon-fixing reactions need light directly, because sugar forms only when the stroma is illuminated.
choices.rationale: The experiment was done entirely in the dark, and sugar formed when ATP and NADPH were added.

choices.label: C
choices.text: ATP alone is enough to drive sugar synthesis, since both additions raise the label slightly.
choices.rationale: ATP alone raised the label from 1 to 2, which is negligible compared with the 60 seen with both.

choices.label: D
choices.text: NADPH alone is enough to drive sugar synthesis because it is the reducing agent.
choices.rationale: NADPH alone gave the same negligible increase, so it cannot drive synthesis without ATP.

title: predict shifts in Calvin cycle intermediates and light-reaction carriers under perturbation
stem: A culture of green algae is photosynthesizing steadily in bright light with a constant supply of CO₂. The light is switched off, and over the next 30 seconds the cells are sampled and the concentrations of the Calvin cycle intermediates 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA) and ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) are measured. Which change is most likely, assuming CO₂ fixation by rubisco continues briefly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both fall, because the Calvin cycle needs light directly to absorb energy.
choices.rationale: The Calvin cycle uses chemical energy carried by ATP and NADPH, not light directly, and the 3-PGA level would rise and not fall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3-PGA rises and RuBP falls, because ATP and NADPH are no longer being made to reduce 3-PGA and regenerate RuBP.
choices.rationale: Correct: rubisco keeps making 3-PGA, but without ATP and NADPH from the light reactions the reduction of 3-PGA and the regeneration of RuBP stop, so 3-PGA accumulates and RuBP is depleted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3-PGA falls and RuBP rises, because carbon is no longer being fixed.
choices.rationale: This is the pattern after removal of CO₂ in the light, and the stem says the CO₂ supply is constant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither changes, because the Calvin cycle is independent of light.
choices.rationale: The Calvin cycle is light independent only in that it does not absorb light, but it relies on the products of the light reactions, so its intermediates change.

title: predict shifts in Calvin cycle intermediates and light-reaction carriers under perturbation (variant 1)
stem: The same algae photosynthesize steadily in bright light. The CO₂ supply is suddenly removed while the light stays on. Over the next 30 seconds, which change is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: RuBP rises and 3-PGA falls, because 3-PGA is no longer made by fixing CO₂ but continues to be converted and RuBP continues to be regenerated.
choices.rationale: Correct: without CO₂ rubisco cannot combine it with RuBP, so 3-PGA production stops and RuBP is no longer consumed, while the light supplies ATP and NADPH to keep processing the existing pool.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3-PGA rises and RuBP falls, because the light reactions stop without CO₂.
choices.rationale: This pattern results from turning off the light, whereas the light here stays on and supplies ATP and NADPH.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both fall, because the Calvin cycle needs CO₂ for every step.
choices.rationale: RuBP is regenerated using ATP and NADPH and is not consumed without CO₂, so it accumulates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither changes, because the Calvin cycle uses stored carbohydrate and not CO₂.
choices.rationale: The Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ from the environment in every turn, and without a supply the intermediates change.

title: predict shifts in Calvin cycle intermediates and light-reaction carriers under perturbation (variant 2)
stem: In bright light, a drug irreversibly inhibits rubisco in a suspension of chloroplasts, and nothing else is affected. Over the next minute, which change is most likely in the stroma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP and NADPH fall, because the Calvin cycle supplies them to the light reactions.
choices.rationale: The light reactions make ATP and NADPH, and the Calvin cycle uses them, so the levels rise when the cycle stops.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The light reactions speed up, because they no longer need to share energy with the Calvin cycle.
choices.rationale: The light reactions need ADP and NADP⁺, which the Calvin cycle regenerates, so they cannot speed up when the cycle stalls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: ATP and NADPH accumulate while ADP and NADP⁺ fall, so the light reactions slow down.
choices.rationale: Correct: with the Calvin cycle stalled, ATP and NADPH are not consumed, so ADP and NADP⁺ run short and the electron transport chain slows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxygen production continues at the same rate, because the light reactions do not depend on the Calvin cycle.
choices.rationale: The light reactions depend on the supply of NADP⁺ and ADP, so oxygen production eventually falls.

title: predict shifts in Calvin cycle intermediates and light-reaction carriers under perturbation (variant 3)
stem: A compound that makes the thylakoid membrane permeable to H⁺, so the proton gradient cannot build up, is added to illuminated chloroplasts. The compound does not directly block electron transport or the Calvin cycle enzymes. In the short term, which result is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oxygen release continues, but ATP synthesis and sugar formation fall because ATP synthase has no proton gradient to use.
choices.rationale: Correct: electron flow can continue and split water, but without a gradient ATP synthase cannot make ATP, and the Calvin cycle slows for lack of ATP.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxygen production stops, because oxygen evolution requires ATP.
choices.rationale: Oxygen comes from the splitting of water at photosystem II and does not require ATP, so it continues.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sugar synthesis speeds up, because protons now reach the stroma more quickly.
choices.rationale: Sugar synthesis needs ATP, and a dissipated gradient lowers ATP, so synthesis slows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: ATP synthesis increases, because H⁺ crossing the membrane more quickly drives ATP synthase faster.
choices.rationale: ATP synthase is driven by the gradient, and the compound destroys the gradient so ATP synthesis falls.

title: effect of anaerobic conditions, cyanide, lactate and compartmentation on respiration
stem:
Yeast cells in a flask with a constant glucose supply are switched from aerobic to anaerobic conditions. Measurements for the same number of cells are:
Condition | Glucose used (µmol/min) | ATP produced (µmol/min)
Aerobic | 5 | 150
Anaerobic | 45 | 90
Which explanation best accounts for the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Without oxygen, glycolysis stops and the Krebs cycle runs faster to supply the ATP.
choices.rationale: The Krebs cycle also depends on NAD⁺ that the electron transport chain regenerates, so it cannot speed up without oxygen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fermentation yields more ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration, so the cells can use their glucose more freely.
choices.rationale: The data show about 2 ATP per glucose anaerobically versus 30 aerobically, so the yield per glucose is lower.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Without oxygen the electron transport chain cannot regenerate NAD⁺, but fermentation does; glycolysis continues at about 2 ATP per glucose, so far more glucose must be used for ATP.
choices.rationale: Correct: ATP per glucose is 30 aerobically (150/5) and 2 anaerobically (90/45), consistent with fermentation regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue at a low yield.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Without oxygen more glucose enters the mitochondria, where it is oxidized with a higher yield.
choices.rationale: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, and mitochondria cannot run the electron transport chain without oxygen, so more glucose in the mitochondria would not raise the yield.

title: effect of anaerobic conditions, cyanide, lactate and compartmentation on respiration (variant 1)
stem: Intact aerobic human cells are given glucose and oxygen. Cyanide, which blocks the last electron carrier of the electron transport chain, is added. Assume the cells cannot make up for the block by fermentation, and Krebs cycle activity is measured as CO₂ release within a few minutes. Which prediction is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CO₂ release rises, because pyruvate accumulates and enters the Krebs cycle faster.
choices.rationale: The Krebs cycle slows when NAD⁺ is depleted, so pyruvate cannot be processed faster.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CO₂ release is unchanged, because CO₂ is made by decarboxylation reactions that do not depend on oxygen.
choices.rationale: The decarboxylation steps depend on NAD⁺ being regenerated, which requires electron transport and ultimately oxygen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: CO₂ release rises, because the cells increase their oxygen consumption to compensate.
choices.rationale: Cyanide blocks the use of oxygen, so oxygen consumption falls and cannot compensate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: CO₂ release falls, because NADH is no longer oxidized to NAD⁺, so NAD⁺-dependent steps of pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle slow.
choices.rationale: Correct: blocking electron flow leaves NADH unoxidized, depleting NAD⁺ needed by the dehydrogenases of pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, so CO₂ release falls.

title: effect of anaerobic conditions, cyanide, lactate and compartmentation on respiration (variant 2)
stem: During a sprint, a muscle cell's oxygen supply does not keep pace with its ATP demand. Lactate accumulates in the muscle. Which statement best explains the role of lactate formation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lactate formation produces most of the muscle's ATP during the sprint.
choices.rationale: Fermentation makes only about 2 ATP per glucose, so it adds a small amount of ATP compared with aerobic respiration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactate formation generates the oxygen that the cell is missing.
choices.rationale: Lactate formation does not make oxygen, and nothing in the pathway can create oxygen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactate formation lets the electron transport chain run faster by supplying more NADH.
choices.rationale: The pathway consumes NADH, and the electron transport chain is limited by oxygen supply, so it cannot run faster.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Converting pyruvate to lactate oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, which lets glycolysis continue making a small amount of ATP without oxygen.
choices.rationale: Correct: glycolysis needs NAD⁺, and the reduction of pyruvate to lactate regenerates it, so glycolysis can continue to make 2 ATP per glucose.

title: effect of anaerobic conditions, cyanide, lactate and compartmentation on respiration (variant 3)
stem: A researcher isolates intact mitochondria and supplies them with oxygen, ADP and phosphate. When glucose is added, no ATP is made. When pyruvate is added instead, ATP is made. Which explanation is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucose cannot be oxidized in the presence of oxygen, but pyruvate can.
choices.rationale: Glucose is oxidized in cells in the presence of oxygen, and the problem is where the enzymes needed are located.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycolysis, which converts glucose to pyruvate, occurs in the cytosol, whereas pyruvate enters the mitochondrion where its oxidation and the later stages of respiration occur.
choices.rationale: Correct: the enzymes of glycolysis are in the cytosol and are absent from isolated mitochondria, so glucose cannot be processed, while pyruvate enters the matrix and feeds the later stages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondria use pyruvate and not glucose because glucose is too large to be oxidized at all.
choices.rationale: Glucose can be fully oxidized by cells, and the issue is that the first stage of its breakdown occurs outside the mitochondrion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mitochondrial ATP synthase works only with pyruvate as a substrate.
choices.rationale: ATP synthase is driven by a proton gradient and does not require pyruvate itself.
